title: Condensing Graphs via One-Step Gradient Matching

problem.claim: Training deep learning models on large datasets requires substantial time and resources, motivating the construction of small synthetic datasets that support sufficient model training.

gap.claim: Existing condensation approaches are not directly applicable to discrete graph data and are computationally expensive because they use nested optimization.

contributions.claim: The paper models discrete graph structure as a probabilistic model to enable efficient dataset condensation for graph datasets.
The paper proposes one-step gradient matching that performs gradient matching for a single step without training network weights.
The paper provides a theoretical analysis of the one-step gradient matching strategy.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Theoretical analysis shows that the strategy can generate synthetic graphs yielding lower classification loss on real graphs.
Experiments on various graph datasets demonstrate the reported effectiveness and efficiency of the method.

The authors report reducing dataset size by 90% while approximating up to 98% of original performance, and report a 15× speedup over multi-step gradient matching for synthesizing 500 graphs on CIFAR10.

narrative_sequence.summary: Large-scale deep learning training is costly, creating demand for small synthetic training datasets.
Recent image-condensation methods use complex bi-level optimization and multi-step network-gradient matching.
These approaches do not directly fit discrete graph data and incur high computational cost from nested optimization.
The paper introduces probabilistic graph modeling and one-step gradient matching without network-weight training.
The abstract reports theoretical, experimental, compression, performance, and speed results.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the probabilistic graph model or optimization details.
The abstract does not identify the graph datasets, architectures, baselines, or evaluation protocol.
